subtype: Approach: noticing warning signs and taking them seriously [Thinking]
passage:
At the small school in Kumarakom, Francis noticed it in pieces. First Ankita stopped coming to the tea shop after class. Then her lunch box went home full, three days running. On Thursday, when he asked about the district quiz they had trained for all year, she shrugged. “Doesn't matter. Nothing really matters.”
He walked home along the canal, turning it over. Maybe she's just tired, he thought. Everyone has bad weeks. But it wasn't one thing. It was the quiz, the lunch, the tea shop, and now those words. Waiting to see felt like the easy choice, not the right one. If I'm wrong, I'm embarrassed. If I'm right and I wait, that's worse.
He turned round and went back. Mrs Mathew, their class teacher, was still marking in the staffroom. He told her everything, word for word. She thanked him, called Ankita's mother while he was still there and asked her to stay close to Ankita that evening, and said she and the school counsellor would sit with Ankita first thing.

qa.q: What did Ankita say when Francis asked about the quiz?
What was Francis worried about on the walk home?
qa.a: Francis was worried that the changes added up to something serious, and uneasy that waiting would be the easy but wrong choice.

qa.q: What else could Francis do in the coming days?
qa.a: Stay friendly and keep inviting Ankita to the tea shop, while Mrs Mathew and the counsellor lead the real help.

qa.q: How might Mrs Mathew see Francis coming back to the staffroom?
qa.a: Mrs Mathew likely feels grateful and concerned, and takes it seriously enough to call Ankita's mother at once.

grounding: Shows a teen noticing a friend withdraw, leave lunch uneaten and say nothing matters, and deciding the signs are serious enough to act on now.

subtype: Approach: noticing warning signs and taking them seriously [Thinking]
passage:
Felix had known Chen since fourth grade in Vancouver, so he noticed the small things. Chen quit the robotics club without a word. He sat alone at lunch with his tray untouched. In chemistry he had written “what's the point of any of it” in the margin of his notebook, and it didn't look like a joke.
Felix's first thought was that Chen just needed space. Guys don't want a fuss. But then he lined it up in his head: the club, the food, the note, the way Chen didn't laugh at anything any more. Each on its own was nothing. All together, over two weeks, they were a pattern, and a pattern like that was not something you waited out.
At the end of the day he went to Ms Alvarez, the school counsellor, and showed her a photo of the note. She asked a few careful questions, then said she would call Chen in before the last bell and phone his parents today. “You did the right thing, Felix.”

qa.q: What had Chen written in the margin of the notebook?
qa.a: What's the point of any of it.

qa.q: What was Felix thinking before deciding to act?
qa.a: Felix first felt unsure, thinking Chen needed space, then grew worried as the signs lined up into a pattern.

qa.q: What else could Felix do to support Chen now?
qa.a: Sit with Chen at lunch and keep things normal and kind, while the counsellor and parents handle the help.

qa.q: How might Ms Alvarez see Felix's visit?
qa.a: Ms Alvarez sees clear warning signs and a friend who cared enough to speak, which lets her act that same day.

grounding: Shows a teen noticing a friend withdraw, stop eating lunch and write that nothing has a point, and deciding the pattern is serious enough to act on.
